lead: Industrial IoT (IIoT) connects machines, sensors and business software so that production data drives control, maintenance and planning. It exists because a factory already produces the data: motor current, temperature, cycle counts, alarms. IIoT moves that data from a machine to a plant screen and to an order system. Industry 4.0 is the wider idea of cyber-physical production built on this flow. You meet it in automotive plants, food processing, textile mills and power stations. The plant metric is OEE, overall equipment effectiveness.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 sensors and sensor nodes; Unit 3 industrial protocols; Unit 5 data analytics.

blocks.text: Industry 4.0 is cyber-physical production: computation and the physical process are linked so that data changes what the plant does. A plant is organised in levels. At Level 0, sensors measure the process and actuators act on it. A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as temperature or vibration, into a signal. An actuator converts a command into motion, heat or flow.

Level 1 is the PLC (programmable logic controller). It reads inputs and writes outputs in a fixed cycle, often every few milliseconds, and it owns real-time control. Example: stop a conveyor when a guard door opens. Level 2 is SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition). It shows the plant, logs alarms and lets an operator change a setpoint. Level 3 is MES (manufacturing execution system): it turns an order into a production schedule, assigns batches and records which material went into which part. Level 4 is ERP (enterprise resource planning): orders, purchase, stock and finance.

Data moves up as summaries; targets move down. OPC-UA is an integration name for exchanging plant data; see Unit 3 for protocol details. A sensor node on a motor may sample vibration locally and send one feature per minute to the next level. Some syllabi call this industrial automation.
Four building blocks appear in most Industry 4.0 designs. The closed-loop idea is in Chapter 6.4.

items: A digital twin is a software model of a machine or process, kept fed with live data. It lets an engineer test a schedule or estimate wear without stopping the line.
A smart factory uses connected assets, edge computing and analytics to adapt production.
Predictive maintenance uses condition data to estimate when a failure is likely and schedules service before it.
Big data and visualization store long histories from many machines and show OEE, energy per part and alarm frequency on dashboards.

blocks.text: Edge computing processes data near the machine. Cloud computing stores years of data and compares plants. A sensor node on a bearing may send raw vibration to an edge gateway. The gateway computes RMS (root mean square) vibration and sends one reading per minute to the cloud. Edge gives low latency and keeps the line running during a wide area network outage; cloud gives long storage and cross-plant models. Remote monitoring of a distant pump is Chapter 6.5.

Security is a lifecycle. Keep an inventory of devices, set a firmware update policy, and use role-based access control so an operator can change a setpoint but a contractor cannot. Unit 5 owns the mechanisms.
OEE (overall equipment effectiveness) is the plant metric for how much good production a scheduled machine delivers. Define the terms in minutes and parts.

Planned production time is the time the machine is scheduled to make parts. Downtime is scheduled time lost to breakdown, setup or no operator. Run time = planned production time − downtime. Total count is all parts made, including rejects. Good count is parts that meet quality. Ideal cycle time is the fastest stable time per part.
OEE = A × P × Q, where A = Run time ÷ Planned production time, P = (Ideal cycle time × Total count) ÷ Run time, Q = Good count ÷ Total count
blocks.where: A is availability; P is performance; Q is quality; OEE is overall equipment effectiveness. Run time = planned production time − downtime. Ideal cycle time is the fastest stable time per part. All three factors are dimensionless; multiply by 100 for percent.

blocks.text: A machine can be available for the whole shift and still have low OEE if it runs slowly or makes rejects. Performance uses total count. Quality then removes rejects. Convert ideal cycle time to the same unit as run time, usually minutes.

figure.caption: The worked example step by step: 480 min scheduled minus 48 min of downtime leaves 432 min of run time, and the three factors 90.0%, 92.6% and 95.0% multiply to give an OEE of 79.2%.

examples.question: A machine is scheduled for 480 min. It is down for 48 min. It makes 800 parts; 760 are good. Ideal cycle time is 30 s per part. Find availability, performance, quality and OEE.
steps: Planned production time = 480 min; downtime = 48 min.
Ideal cycle time = 30 s = 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 min per part.
examples.answer: Availability is 90.0%, performance is 92.6%, quality is 95.0%, and OEE is 79.2%.
examples.check:
planned = 480
downtime = 48
total = 800
good = 760
ideal_s = 30
run = planned - downtime
availability = run / planned
ideal_min = ideal_s / 60
performance = (ideal_min * total) / run
quality = good / total
oee = availability * performance * quality
print(f"{availability*100:.1f}")
print(f"{performance*100:.1f}")
print(f"{quality*100:.1f}")
print(f"{oee*100:.1f}")

traps: Performance uses total count, not good count; quality applies the good count. Mixing them double-counts rejects.
Convert ideal cycle time to the same unit as run time. 30 s is 0.5 min, not 30 min.
OEE is not the same as availability. A machine can be available for 100% of scheduled time and still have low OEE from slow cycles or rejects.
Downtime is subtracted from planned production time, not from 24 hours. Use the schedule you are measuring.
SCADA is supervision, not real-time control; the PLC closes the control loop. Do not credit SCADA with millisecond actuation.

quiz.q: List the five automation levels from field device to business planning and give one function for each.
quiz.a: Level 0 sensors/actuators: measure and act; Level 1 PLC: real-time control; Level 2 SCADA: supervision and alarms; Level 3 MES: production schedule and genealogy; Level 4 ERP: orders and finance.

quiz.q: Why does a digital twin need live data, not only a CAD model?
quiz.a: A CAD model gives geometry. A twin must mirror current state and behaviour, so live sensor data updates it and lets you test decisions against the real process.

quiz.q: Planned production time is 600 min. Downtime is 60 min. Total count is 900 parts; 855 are good. Ideal cycle time is 20 s per part. Find availability, performance, quality and OEE.
A plant adds vibration sensors and an edge gateway but still sends only daily OEE to ERP. Has it become Industry 4.0? Explain using the hierarchy.
quiz.a: Partly. It has Level 0 sensing and edge processing, but the data is not feeding MES or ERP decisions in a closed loop. Industry 4.0 needs cyber-physical feedback and business integration, not only a dashboard.

quiz.q: Give one reason to compute a feature at the edge and one reason to store raw data in the cloud.
quiz.a: Edge: low latency and operation during a wide area network outage. Cloud: long history and cross-plant models.

quiz.q: Define OEE and name its three factors.
quiz.a: OEE is overall equipment effectiveness, the product of availability, performance and quality.

quiz.q: A line has availability 0.85, performance 0.90 and quality 0.96. Find OEE.

beyond: Not for the exam. The automation hierarchy is standardised in ISA-95 (also published as IEC 62264), which names levels 0 to 4 in a similar way. Industry 4.0 reference work uses RAMI 4.0 and the Asset Administration Shell to describe assets and their digital representatives. A digital thread links design, production and service records for one part. Search for ISA-95 levels, RAMI 4.0, Asset Administration Shell, digital thread and edge AI for condition monitoring.
